"Whenever you roll one or more dice" triggers (Barbarian Class, the Fallout and
AFR roll-a-die block): the `dice_rolled` event exists and carries `results` and
`sides`, and nothing subscribes to it — a name in `TRIGGER_EVENTS` away, plus a
decision about which bindings a trigger's effects can read. And the AFR d20
outcome tables ("1—9 … 10—19 … 20"), which are a banding construct on top of a
roll and their own capability.

### Test

`tests/unit/test_dice_rolling.py` — 39 tests. The claim classes are
`TestOneRollReadTwoWays` (the evens and the sixes come off the same faces; a read
draws no randomness; every face is counted exactly once),
`TestTheBindingIsFacesNotObjects` (the trap above, asserted from both directions),
`TestZeroDice`, `TestRerolling`, `TestDeterminism`, `TestTheEvent`,
`TestThroughARealCard` (`t_bobblehead`, the ability activated with the RNG pinned,
so the Treasures are checked against the faces that actually came up) and
`TestTheLoaderGuards`.

See `docs/card-dsl.md` ("Rolling dice") and `docs/rules-coverage.md`.

## Systematic card support — the deck finished

### Overview

Deck import shipped and immediately exposed the real problem: a real imported
deck had **41 of its 100 cards doing nothing**. The proxy generator gives every
card its name, art, cost, types and keywords, but the rules text is inert. That
is honest, and it is not a game.

MTG has tens of thousands of cards. Hand-writing them does not scale, so this is
a repeatable batch: read a card's oracle text, emit a structured DSL object, and
**refuse to ship any that cannot prove it works**.

Full design in [card-authoring.md](card-authoring.md).

### What shipped

**Playable cards: 230 → 732.** Written by the pipeline, committed to
`data/cards/auto/`, re-verified on every test run.

- **A verifier with six gates**, which is the centre of the design rather than
  the generator. `compile_card` validates *vocabulary*, not *meaning* — a card
  can say "draw two cards", do `gain_life`, and compile, cast and resolve without
  raising. So every candidate must come with an assertion about the board and
  demonstrate it. `tests/cards/test_authoring.py` has that exact case.
- **A priority queue**: cards from a deck somebody imported first, then EDHREC
  rank. It records *why* each card failed, so the tail is a roadmap rather than a
  mystery — `--report` prints it.
- **A deterministic template tier**, free and exact, covering the sentence shapes
  common enough to be worth a rule.

**Auras and Equipment** — the largest block in the catalog, ~1,700 cards. Most of
the object model already existed; what was missing was an Aura *attaching to what
its spell targeted* (after placement, because `reset_permanent_state` clears
`attached_to` on the way in — so an Aura attaching itself during `spell_effects`
arrives enchanting nothing and is silently binned), and a static that reads
`{"attached": true}`. Equipment needed no engine work at all: `Equip {2}` is a
sorcery-speed activated ability whose effect is the existing `attach` op.

**Devoid, Changeling and Prowess** turned out to need none either — the first is
self-implementing, the second is `add_subtype`, the third is a `spell_cast`
trigger the DSL has always been able to say.

**The agent loop** — self-contained work packets on disk, so a Claude Code
session and an unattended API worker read the identical file and write the
identical answer.

### The imported deck, card by card

The headline metric for this work is the deck that started it
(`moxfield.com/decks/brDuu9c6_0yuaoHLijLFHw`). It began at **41 of 100 cards
doing nothing**. It is now at **zero**: all 72 distinct cards play.

Each of the following was a *mechanic* rather than effort, and each shipped with
its own unit tests and a `card-dsl.md` entry:

| Mechanic | Card that needed it |
|---|---|
| Delayed triggers (`delay`) | Arcane Denial, Nezahal |
| Kicker | Into the Roil |
| Modal spells with a shared optional target | Simic Charm, Koma |
| "Its activated abilities can't be activated" (`lock_abilities`) | Koma |
| `else`/`condition`/`repeat` on `may` | Coral Atoll, Jungle Basin, Cultivator Colossus |
| Filtering a `binding` — "is the card I revealed a land?" | Coiling Oracle |
| `*/*` via a static `set_pt` reading the board | Cultivator Colossus |
| `set_types` plus "as long as" conditions on counters | Arixmethes |
| `double_land_triggers` | Ancient Greenwarden |
| `cost_reduction` | Ghalta |
| Monstrosity and `freeze` | Shipbreaker Kraken |
| Token copies (`copy_permanent`) | Scute Swarm, Spitting Image |
| Protection, across damage / enchant / block / target | Greensleeves |
| `not_cause` loop guard, and Partner as an inert keyword | Kodama of the East Tree |
| `double_land_mana`, `freeze_opponent_lands`, `skip_next_untap` | Vorinclex |
| Hybrid mana in the payment solver | Spitting Image |
| Restricted mana and granted abilities | Herd Heirloom |
| Restricted mana naming the *chosen* type, and reaching ability costs | Secluded Courtyard |
| Retrace — casting from the graveyard | Spitting Image |
| Suspend — a special action, an upkeep rule, and a free cast | Search for Tomorrow |
| `two_piles` — the one decision an opponent makes | Fact or Fiction |

One of those found a real bug rather than a gap: `self_enters` and
`permanent_enters` are the same engine event, separated only by `source: "self"`,
so a card omitting it fired on *every* permanent entering. Every hand-written
card had it; three new ones did not. The loader now supplies it, because the name
can only mean one thing.

### What the last eight cost

The three that reached into `mana.py` were the risk, and each was landed on its
own with the 160-game arena run in between rather than all at once:

- **Hybrid mana** (625 catalog cards) is additive to `Requirement`, with the
  no-hybrid fast path left exactly as it was — it runs in the solver's inner loop
  on every priority window. Assignment is exhaustive and shared by `satisfies`
  and `ManaPool.spend`, because with one white and one blue, `{W/U}{W/U}` is
  payable only if the two pips take different symbols. The proxy stopped
  narrowing hybrid costs as a result, so imported decks keep their real ones.
- **Restricted mana** (162) never touches the solver at all: sources that may not
  pay for this spell are filtered out before it runs. That works only because
  mana here is tapped at the moment it is spent.

  Extended twice since, both for Secluded Courtyard's one printed line. The
  restriction can name **the type its own permanent chose**, so it is resolved
  per permanent when the mana is offered instead of frozen at load — every fixed
  value would be a different card, and `"creature"` in particular would be
  strictly better than printed. And it can permit **activating an ability** and
  not only casting, which needed a second purpose (`costs.ability_purpose`)
  threaded through `legality._ability_aims` and `game._activate` the way
  `spell_purpose` was already threaded through the four cast sites. The purpose
  carries *which action* it is, and that is the load-bearing half: an activate
  permission matched on names alone would have silently rewritten Herd Heirloom
  and Master of Dark Rites, both of which print "only to **cast**".
- **Vorinclex's doubling** had to be computed in two places — `_sources_of` so
  legality counts it, `activate_mana_ability` so payment adds it — and a
  disagreement would strand a spell mid-cast. One `mana_produced` helper, called
  from both, plus a test that casts an 8-drop off four doubled Forests.

Two things were deliberately **not** done, and fail loudly instead of silently:
granting a *static* or *activated* ability (the loader rejects it rather than
compiling something legality would never offer), and phyrexian mana (a life
payment, not a colour choice). *Phyrexian mana has since shipped — see the
`{W/P}` section at the top of this file.*

### What is left, beyond this deck

Across the whole catalog `--report` ranks **Flashback** (234), **Crew** (74),
**Cycling** (71), **Ward** (41) and **Convoke** (39) as the biggest remaining
blocks by card count. Flashback in particular is now nearly free: it is retrace's
machinery — casting from the graveyard — with a different additional cost.

## All Card Support — done

### Overview
- The application was written to support just 2 precon decks
- Because of this, only cards in these 2 pre-cons are supported to display
- The import command needs to be extended to include all possible cards (art work and basic information)
- This information will be used to support the 2 additional precons planned in the new redesign
- In addition, this should offer general support for moxfield deck looking up so that users can choose their own custom deck when starting a game

### Task
- Add support for all cards, 2 additional precons (Isperia, Supreme Judge and zurgo stormrender), and custom decks via Moxfield deck import

### What shipped

**Custom decks via Moxfield, end to end.** Paste a public deck link and play it.
The whole loop is documented in [deck-import.md](deck-import.md); the short
version is that `api2.moxfield.com/v3/decks/all/{publicId}` is open to a scripted
client (the 403 recorded in the design record (`docs/design-record.md#board-themes`) was a *different* endpoint), and
every card characteristic comes from our own catalog rather than from the payload.

**"All cards" was mostly a catalog problem, and it split in two.** `cards.sqlite`
already held every English card; what was limited to the precons was the *engine
registry*, the ~149 hand-written cards. So the work was:

- Three columns on the catalog — `oracle_text`, `keywords`, `produced_mana`.
  Without the last, a generated land taps for nothing and a deck of inert lands
  is not a deck. The index grew 7.3 MB → 14.4 MB.
- A **key fix that mattered more than it looks**: the table was keyed on `name`
  alone, so 87 real cards printed with a same-named token — Tarmogoyf, Champion
  of Wits, Adorned Pouncer — had been evicted by it and were unreachable. Now
  keyed on `(name, is_token)`.
- `cards/proxy.py`, which generates a playable definition for a card nobody
  wrote: real name, art, cost, types, stats, keywords and mana abilities, with
  the rest of the rules text inert *and listed*. All 32,827 catalog rows
  generate and compile.
- A **two-layer registry**. `default_registry()` is the authored pool and is what
  every test and the trainer see; `server_registry()` adds `data/generated/`.
  Without the split, `pytest` would answer differently depending on what somebody
  imported last week.

### The two precons

**Isperia, Supreme Judge** and **Zurgo Stormrender** ship, hand-written, at the
Aesi/Edgar bar: every card in both is implemented and covered by
`test_every_card_works`. 81 new card definitions, 230 in the registry, and the
artless set is still exactly five. See [decks.md](decks.md).

Neither commander's own text was expressible before, and none of the three
engine additions is visible in a two-player game — which is why the original two
decks never wanted them:

- `defending` on an `attacks` trigger — *"whenever a creature attacks **you**"*.
  `controller` answers whose creature is swinging, a different question; written
  with `controller: "opponent"` Isperia draws a card when one opponent attacks
  another.
- `attacking` on `create_token` — a token put onto the battlefield already in
  combat, against whoever its maker is attacking. That is mobilize. It is not a
  *declared* attacker, which is the real rule and also what stops it making
  another token forever.
- `was_attacking` on `leaves_battlefield` — last-known information, snapshotted
  where `was_creature` already was, because by the time the trigger resolves the
  object is out of combat and there is nothing left to ask. That is Zurgo's
  second ability.

All three have tests in `tests/unit/test_attack_triggers.py`, several of which
need a three-player pod to mean anything.

**Three cards were dropped rather than shipped wrong**, and the reasons are worth
keeping: Isperia's pillowfort (Propaganda, Ghostly Prison) needs a cost-to-attack
mechanic the engine does not have; Condemn's only legal target is an attacking
creature, which the `test_every_card_works` sandbox has no way to produce; and
Village Rites puts a sacrifice in its casting cost, which the DSL only models on
an activated ability. Each would have been an inert card that looked implemented.

## Progressive Zoom — done

### Overview
- The game typically starts with very few cards and ends with very many
- This leads to poor use of screen real estate early in the game as the benifit of being able to show the game state end game
- Instead, the board zooms (both user and CPU) + cards in hand could use a more intelligent zoom system that tries to maximize readability at all stages of the game

### What shipped

**A measured fit solver, not a lookup table.** `frontend/src/logic/zoomFit.ts` is a
pure module that shelf-packs each lane's real footprints — a tapped permanent is
landscape, a stack of basics is one box, a host carries its auras — and returns the
largest card width whose wrapped rows still fit a given height.
`frontend/src/state/useZoomFit.ts` supplies the measurements and applies the
answer through the `cardScale` prop that already ran `Table` → `PlayerMat` → `Lane`.

A count→ratio table was the obvious alternative and it cannot work: it has no idea
whether slack exists. There is 580px of lane budget at 2560×1278 and 160px at
1600×700, and no function of card count knows the difference.

**The measurements say the win is asymmetric, and it is a win in both directions:**

| | 1600×950 | 2560×1278 | 1600×700 |
|---|---|---|---|
| board card, before | 87.4px | 110px | 68px |
| board card, after | 88.9px | **150px** | **52px** |
| lane budget | 305px | 584px | 160px |

At 2560×1278 the board grows 36% into space that was simply being wasted. At
1600×700 it *shrinks* 24%, because the honest answer on a cramped screen is smaller
cards rather than a board you have to scroll. At 1600×950 it barely moves, and the
reason is worth writing down: the empty board already needs 304px of a 305px budget.

**Opponents scale with the viewer, never past it.** Their ceiling is the viewer's
solved width times the existing seat ratio, so the designed proportion holds and a
one-opponent pod with two lands cannot render cards bigger than your own. Each mat
is solved for its own fullness and the fullest sets the size for the row.

### The real ceiling on this, and it is not the solver

**The orb columns own the vertical space.** At 1600×950 the viewer's `.mat__side` is
330px — taller than its own lanes at 299px — and the compact orb is 297px. Together
the two consume 627px of a 649px play area, and the cards get the remainder. That is
why the gain at the most common viewport is ~2%: there is nothing to give.

Worse, the orb's mana row grows as lands are played, so mid-game the viewer's mat
can hide 150px of itself and no card size fixes it, because the overflow is not the
cards. Making that column fluid — or moving the piles out of it — is the change that
would unlock 1600×950, and it is a separate piece of work.

### Deliberate divergence from the plan

The plan called for a binary search. `boardHeight` turns out **not** to be monotone
in card width: a tapped permanent is shorter but wider, so growing the cards can push
a tall card onto the next row and leave a short row behind it, making the lane
briefly *shorter*. Bisection over that returns a size that overflows, silently. It is
a descending scan instead, and `tests/zoomFit.test.ts` pins the counter-example.

The plan also called for rewriting `CardStack`'s container and `HandFan`'s slot pitch
as `calc()` so they could animate. Neither was needed: `--card-w` is a registered
`<length>`, so transitioning it animates every declaration that reads it, and a plain
CSS transition on the two JS-set properties covers the rest.

### Guarded by
Four cases in `frontend/e2e/layout.spec.ts` — the zoom responds on a big display, no
card leaves the 52–150px legibility band, the zoom never grows the board under the
hand at any point in a game, and an opponent's board filling up does not move yours.
`tests/zoomFit.test.ts` holds the wrap model to the *real rendered lane heights* at
three viewports, which is the assertion that caught the model being wrong by 19px per
front lane.

The pre-existing "the viewer's bands do not move" case now pins the zoom
(`startGame(page, { zoomLock: true })`). Progressive zoom moves those bands on
purpose, so with it live that assertion would have had to be loosened past the point
of catching the collapsing lane it exists for.

---

## Standardize Card Placement — done

### Overview
- The board used to render four full-width rows in the same order on every mat,
  with the lands furthest from the player who controls them
- That is the opposite of how the game is physically played: your mana sits in
  the row nearest you, and creatures go out front
- Creatures and enchantments were also split into separate rows, when on a table
  they sit side by side

### What shipped
- **Two bands per mat.** Creatures (with planeswalkers) beside the global
  artifacts and enchantments across the front, split 2:1 because that is where
  the cards accumulate; lands in the band behind them. They remain two separate
  drop targets — only the row is shared.
- **Lands nearest their controller.** `LANES` in
  `frontend/src/logic/zoneGrouping.ts` is now declared front to back, so the
  array is the layout.
- **Opponent mats are mirrored** (`PlayerMat`'s `mirrored` prop). Their lands sit
  against their own edge of the screen, which puts the two creature bands either
  side of the table's midline and makes combat read as a line.
- **Auras and equipment are tucked under their host**, not loose in the
  enchantment zone. `attachmentsFor` pulls anything attached to a permanent on
  the same mat out of the lanes and `CardStack` draws it peeking out from
  underneath, still individually hoverable and clickable. An attachment whose
  host is on somebody else's board stays a loose card rather than vanishing.
- **Your own board holds still.** All three of the viewer's lanes render at a
  full card's height whether or not they hold anything, and the orb's mana row
  has a reserved slot. Before this, playing your first creature shoved the land
  row down by a whole card, killing it shoved the row back up, and tapping mana
  did it again several times a turn. The cost is one card height of empty slot
  on a mat that fills anyway.

### Known limit — fixed by Progressive Zoom
Opponent mats used to be content-sized, so an opponent's board growing translated
your board down the screen. The fix was the one this section predicted: compact
mats now get a fixed lane height (`--pod-lanes-h`) and scroll inside it, using the
fade affordance on `.mat--compact .mat__lanes` that already existed for it, rather
than reserving width they do not have. Guarded by "an opponent's board filling up
does not move the viewer's board" in `frontend/e2e/layout.spec.ts`.

Reserving their *lanes* is still not done, and the measurement that argued against
it still stands — a compact mat has about 158px of lane width against a 51px card,
so an always-present global lane wrapped their creatures onto an extra row. What
has changed is that it is no longer a layout-stability question, only a width one:
hiding an empty lane cannot move the mat's box any more. `PlayerMat`'s `visible`
is a pure width optimisation now.

**Shipping Isperia and Zurgo made the remaining half of this measurable.** A pod
used to be one deck three times over, because opponent seats cycle whatever
`/api/decks` returns and there were only two. With four decks a pod is genuinely
four different boards, and Zurgo's is a token deck: an opponent mat then hides
about **two** card rows behind its scroll rather than the under-one the fixed
lane height was sized for (136px hidden against a 73px card, measured).

Nothing regressed — the layout code is untouched and the row still never clips.
What changed is that the worst realistic case got worse, and it is now
reproducible instead of hypothetical. `frontend/e2e/cycle3.spec.ts`'s "opponent
cards shrink with the pod" pins its pod to two decks so it keeps measuring card
*sizing*, which is what it was written for; the row-budget question wants its own
test and a taller `--pod-lanes-h` for four-player pods.

### Deliberate divergence from the reference layout
The reference diagram puts library / graveyard / exile in a strip beside the
lands. They stay in the orb column instead: graveyard and exile are consulted
rarely enough that the width is better spent on the board, and the orb already
gives each one a labelled pile.

Guarded by two cases in `frontend/e2e/layout.spec.ts`: "lands sit nearest the
player who controls them" and "the viewer's bands do not move as permanents
enter and leave play". Both band orders render perfectly well and a jumping
board renders perfectly well, so only a measurement notices a regression.

## `grant_rebound` — the rider read off the wrong object

### Overview

Ojer Pakpatiq, Deepest Epoch: "Whenever you cast an instant spell from your
hand, **it gains rebound**."

The gap record filed against this said rebound was "absent from the 34-entry
keywords list", which is true, and concluded the mechanic had "no behaviour
behind it", which was not. Rebound has been complete since `CardDef.rebound`
existed — the exile-on-resolution rider in `_place_after_resolution`, the
`rebound_by` mark on the exiled card, and the free cast at the controller's next
upkeep in `suspend.rebound_tick`. It is a **card-level rider**, not a keyword,
which is why looking in the keyword list found nothing and why the packet now
names `CARD_LEVEL_RIDER_KEYS` explicitly.

What was genuinely missing was one word of scope. The rider asked `card.rebound`
— what a spell says about *itself* — so only a card that printed the keyword
could ever have it, and no effect could hand it to a spell that did not.

### The change

`granted_rebound` on the spell's `GameObject`, set while the spell is still on
the stack, read beside the card flag:

```python
rebounds = (
    (card.rebound or obj.granted_rebound)
    and obj.cast_from_hand
    and destination is Zone.GRAVEYARD
)
```

That disjunction is the whole feature. It is the same shape `playable_exiles`
already has beside `card.graveyard_cast_exiles` on the neighbouring line: the
card field is what the spell says about itself, the object field is what somebody
else said about it, and the rider is not entitled to care which.

Deliberately *no* second path. A granted rebound could have been built as its own
exile-plus-delayed-trigger, and that would have been two mechanisms for one
behaviour — the mistake made once already for Lier's granted flashback and
reverted, where `graveyard_cast_exiles` turned out to be doing the work all along.

### The stack is the only window

The flag has to be written while the spell is on the stack. `_place_after_resolution`
consults it during resolution, and by the time any later effect could reach the
object the stack list has been popped — which is the same reason `encode` is a
rider rather than an `exile` written into `spell_effects`, and the same reason
Mizzix's Mastery's "Exile Mizzix's Mastery" is `exiles_itself` rather than an op.

Addressing it was free: `spell_cast` is in `OBJECT_SUBJECT_TRIGGERS`, so the
trigger already binds the cast spell's `sid`. `copy_spell` had the lookup inline
with a comment arguing that a second spelling would be a second bug; `grant_rebound`
asking the same question a third time is where that stopped being hypothetical,
so it is now `_spell_named_by` and both ops call it.

### The from-hand gate, twice

702.87a says "if you cast this spell from your hand", and the gate is also the
loop guard: the free cast at the next upkeep is made **from exile**, so without
it one instant would rebound at every upkeep for the rest of the game.
`suspend.rebound_tick` clears the mark before casting for the same reason — the
free cast is itself a cast.

Because the gate lives in the rider rather than in the op, a grant made to a
spell cast from anywhere else is **inert rather than refused**. That is what lets
Ojer Pakpatiq's printed "from your hand" live in the trigger's filter without the
op having to re-check it, and it means the granted card cannot rebound its own
rebound.

### Tests

`tests/unit/test_granted_rebound.py`, eleven of them. The load-bearing one is
`TestPrintedReboundIsUnchanged`: without a control that a card printing rebound
still rebounds with no granter on the board, every other assertion here is also
consistent with the bait card having had rebound all along.

## `mana_restriction` learns the word "non"

### Overview

The Emperor of Palamecia: "{T}: Add {U} or {R}. **Spend this mana only to cast a
noncreature spell.**"

`mana_restriction` was already the right home for the line, and it was purely
positive. `_restriction_groups` compiled each group to a frozenset of literal
lowercased type and subtype names, and `ManaSource.permits` answered
`group <= purpose.names` against the flat set of the spell's own types and
subtypes. Nothing anywhere in that chain could ask whether a name was **absent**.

The worker that found this had been told by me that `mana_restriction` would
carry it. It read the source instead of taking that on trust, and reported back
that it would not — which is the whole reason the gap record was worth having.

### Both near misses are wrong, in opposite directions

This is the useful part, because a negation is only worth building if the
spellings already available are worse:

- **`["noncreature"]`** loads. The loader's guard on a restriction entry only
  asks that it look like a word, deliberately, because subtypes are open-ended
  and there is no closed list to check against. So the card compiles, and then
  matches nothing for ever — no spell has a type called "noncreature". The mana
  becomes permanently unspendable: a strictly *worse* card than printed, and a
  silent one, which the loader's own comment already flagged as the failure mode
  a typo produces.
- **`["artifact", "enchantment", "instant", "sorcery"]`** enumerates the
  noncreature types as an any-of, and over-permits every artifact creature and
  enchantment creature spell — `permits` sees `artifact` among the purpose's
  names, finds its one-name group satisfied, and never learns that `creature` is
  in that same set. A strictly *better* card.

Both are kept as live cards in `tests/unit/test_mana_restriction_not.py`. The
sharpest pair in the file is the same artifact creature spell against the two
fonts: castable under the enumeration, not castable under the negation, same
board, same spell.

### The change

`RestrictionGroup(required, forbidden)` replaces the bare frozenset, and a group
is satisfied when `required <= names and not (forbidden & names)`. Four call
sites, all of them named by the gap record before a line was written: the loader
builds it, `ManaRestriction.dynamic` scans both halves for the chosen-type
sentinel, `costs._resolve_groups` substitutes into both, and `permits` asks both.

A bare frozenset is still accepted and coerced, because that *is* the shorthand —
every name required, none forbidden — and because coercing is one line against
rewriting every construction that predates the change.

Two refusals rather than two silent acceptances:

- A name both required and forbidden in one group. Nothing satisfies it, which is
  the same dead mana the typo makes, so it is a load error rather than a card
  that quietly does nothing.
- A negated `{"chosen_type_of": …}`. No card prints "spend this only to cast a
  spell that is *not* the chosen type", and accepting it would mean a sentinel
  that only half the substitution path honours. `_resolve_groups` substitutes
  into `forbidden` anyway, so the day one is printed this is not the place that
  kept the sentinel.

### Where the idea came from

Trigger filters have had `not_types` all along, and selectors have
`not_types`/`not_subtypes`. The restriction language was the one place the
negation was missing, and it is the same one word.

## A "you may play it" permission with a real duration

### Overview

Two cards, one missing idea:

- "Exile the top card of your library. You may play it **until your next end
  step**." (Haste Magic.)
- "Exile the top two cards of your library. **Until the end of your next turn**,
  you may play those cards." (Light Up the Stage.)

The engine had exactly one clock: `playable_turn` on the object, compared against
`state.turn` in seven places. That is the impulse-draw "this turn", and it is
correct for the family it was built for.

### Why this is not a rounding error

The interesting thing about this gap is its direction. Almost every approximation
worth refusing makes a **better** card than printed; this one makes a worse one.

Haste Magic is an instant. Cast on an opponent's turn — a normal line of play —
the printed card lets you play the exiled card through the rest of that turn,
every other player's turn, and your following turn up to its end step.
`playable_this_turn` revokes it at the turn boundary. Nothing on the board shows
a permission expiring early, so the loss is silent, and the card looks
implemented.

Going the other way is no better: `grant_playable` carries no duration at all,
which is an open-ended permission.

### The clocks are keyed to the player, not to a turn number

Neither duration computes a future turn number, and the reason is written in
`_untap_step` already: eliminating a player moves everybody else's "next turn",
and extra turns move it again. So both are ended when the grantee's step arrives,
exactly as detain, goad, "until your next turn" block prohibitions, player
protections and life locks all are.

`turn._expire_permissions` is called twice in `begin_step` — as the end step
begins, and in cleanup.

### One word apart

The two clocks differ only in "next", and it changes both hooks:

- **"your next end step"** asked on your own turn is *this* turn's, so the
  permission is no longer than the this-turn one. The hook clears
  unconditionally when the grantee's end step begins. A card exiled *during* your
  own end step therefore survives to the following turn's — correct, because the
  end step you are standing in is not your next one, and the hook for it has
  already run.
- **"your next turn"** is never the turn you are standing in. So the cleanup hook
  checks `playable_turn < state.turn` as well as the seat: without that, a card
  exiled on your own turn would lose its permission at the end of the turn it was
  granted in, which is the shorter card again.

### Seven readers, one question

`playable_turn == state.turn` appeared in legality, both cast paths, the any-type
relaxation, the group ledger and the flashback rider. That comparison *is* the
this-turn duration, so generalising meant replacing all seven with
`GameObject.playable_live(turn)` rather than adding an eighth reader that knew
about durations while the others did not.

### A test that was wrong before the engine was

Three of the tests in `tests/unit/test_playable_duration.py` failed on first run,
and none of them was an engine bug. `pass_until` returns the moment it finds no
pending decision, so on a game built with `advance=False` the "hand the turn to
the opponent" helper did nothing at all — every "granted on an opponent's turn"
test was quietly testing the other case. Reaching the opponent's precombat main
was then still not enough, because seat 0 has to *hold priority* there to cast an
instant; the condition has to be the cast action, not the step. And the
opponent's-end-step assertion navigated to a cleanup step, which grants no
priority, so `pass_until` sailed through it and on into the grantee's own end
step — where the permission correctly ended, looking exactly like a bug. That one
now applies the hook directly, which is the actual claim: same state, opponent
active, permission untouched.

## `grant_graveyard_cast` — a permission that outlives the permanent granting it

### Overview

Urabrask, chapter III: "Until end of turn, you may cast instant and sorcery
spells from any graveyard. If a spell cast this way would be put into a
graveyard, exile it instead." Yawgmoth's Will is the same card.

The engine had exactly one graveyard-cast permission — `cast_from_graveyard`, a
static — and it is the wrong shape three ways over for this sentence. They are
the same three ways `BlockProhibition` inverted for "can't block", which is why
this ended up in the same place:

- **It needs a permanent on the battlefield.** The chapter exiles the Saga in the
  same breath as granting the permission.
- **It has no clock.** This one ends with the turn.
- **It reaches its controller's own graveyard.** This one reaches the table.

### The spec is a static, deliberately

The grant stores an ordinary `cast_from_graveyard` static dict and
`graveyard_cast_permissions` yields it beside the real ones. That single decision
is most of the feature:

- `affects_spells` filters the cards — existing code.
- `max_per_turn` and `grants_flashback` meter it — existing code, including the
  uncapped-permission argument built for Lier.
- The spell is marked `cast_from_graveyard` when cast, so
  `graveyard_cast_exiles` exiles it as it resolves — which means **the second
  printed sentence needed no code at all.**

The loader therefore asks for the same two guarantees the static's own loader
does, in the same words: a filter, because an absent one frees the whole
graveyard; and either a cap or `grants_flashback`, because a permission that
neither meters nor exiles is an engine rather than a printed line.

### The source survives its zone

`GraveyardCastGrant` keeps the granting oid even though the Saga is in exile, and
that is not sentiment. The rate limit is counted per granting object in the turn
ledger, and `graveyard_cast_allows` resolves a `chosen_type` against the granter.
Both keep working, because a `GameObject` outlives the zone it was in — the same
property `rebound_by` and `exiled_by` rely on.

### `any_graveyard` is asked twice

Once to widen the candidate loop past the caster's own graveyard, and once per
card in `_graveyard_cast_permission`. Both are load-bearing: widening alone would
offer a card that no permission actually covers, and asking alone would never see
the card, because the loop over graveyards is where candidates come from. The
per-card half is what keeps Edgar and flashback out of an opponent's graveyard.

### Why not `grant_playable`

It is the near miss, and it very nearly works — it takes an arbitrary selector,
it is turn-scoped, and `as_flashback` already produces the exile. The gap record
argued it could not name "every graveyard", which was not quite the real problem.

The real problem is that it **snapshots**. It marks the cards it can see when it
resolves. A spell that reaches a graveyard later in the same turn is castable
under the printed card and invisible to a mark placed earlier. For a card whose
whole point is a graveyard that refills as you empty it, that is not an
approximation — it is the loop, deleted.

`TestACardThatArrivesLater` is that difference, asserted.

## Counting spells by type, not just counting them

### Overview

Urabrask's front face: "{R}: Exile Urabrask, then return it to the battlefield
transformed… Activate only as a sorcery and only if you've cast **three or more
instant and/or sorcery spells** this turn."

Two workers disagreed about this line, which is the useful part of the story. The
first authored around it and reported the front face expressible, blocking only on
chapter III. The second read `values.py` and `structs.py` and reported that
`spells_cast_this_turn` sums `TurnLedger.spells_cast` — a flat per-player integer
bumped once per `SPELL_CAST` event with no record of *what* was cast — so there is
nothing to filter on and the condition would turn on after three creature spells.

The second was right, and the disagreement is worth recording because the first
reading is the natural one: the value has a plausible name, it takes a player
spec, and nothing about it advertises that it has thrown the types away.

### The change

`TurnLedger.spells_cast_ids` — the printed id of each spell, in cast order, per
caster — kept **beside** the count rather than replacing it. Storm reads the bare
count and reads it once per copy; making every storm trigger walk a list to serve
a rarer question would be the wrong trade, and the two answers cannot drift
because they are written from the same event.

The id recorded is `data["card"]`, which is the face that was cast: a disturb cast
turns the card over inside `push_spell`, and the half that was cast is the half
the condition is asking about.

Matching is `_matches_printed`, the same matcher `graveyard_cast_allows` uses, and
for its stated reason — a spell that has finished resolving has a printed face and
no board state left to ask about.

### Where the filter lives

Inside the value, not beside it:

```jsonc
{ "spells_cast_this_turn": { "player": "you", "filter": { … } } }
```

A sibling `filter` key would have to be added to `VALUE_KEYS`, and would then be
silently legal on every value expression in the language. `permanents_entered_this_turn`
already set the precedent of a ledger read that takes a filter rather than a bare
player spec.

The branch is on the presence of `filter`, not on the type of the value, because a
player spec is itself sometimes a mapping — `{"except": …}` — and typing the
branch would have quietly changed what those mean.

### Tests

`tests/unit/test_spells_cast_by_type.py`. The load-bearing pair casts three
creature spells and asserts the bare count reaches 3 while the filtered one stays
0 — which is the second worker's argument, executable.

## Plot — a rider and a permission, both already built

### Overview

Lilah, Undefeated Slickshot: "Whenever you cast a multicolored instant or sorcery
spell from your hand, exile that spell instead of putting it into your graveyard
as it resolves. If you do, it becomes plotted." Plot (702.171a) is "you may cast
it as a sorcery on a later turn without paying its mana cost."

The gap record filed three needs. Two of them were shapes this session had
already built for other cards, which is the interesting part — the third was one
word.

### The rider is `grant_rebound`'s slot

`grant_plot` writes a flag on the spell's object while it is still on the stack;
`_place_after_resolution` reads it and sends the spell to exile instead of the
graveyard; and the permission is written **after** the move, because
`reset_permanent_state` runs on the way and clears every `playable_*` field —
which is the ordering `rebound_by` and `exiled_by` both discovered first.

Rebound and plot differ only in what they leave behind: one free cast owed at the
next upkeep, against a standing permission with no end. Everything else is the
same slot, which is why plot needed no new machinery for its first sentence.

It has to be a rider rather than an `exile` written into the ability's effects,
for the reason `encode` and `exiles_itself` both give: by the time an ability's
effects run, the stack list is already popped, so the op would reach nothing and
the printed line would silently do nothing.

### The permission is three riders on one that existed

- **`later_turns`** — the fourth `playable_duration`, and the only one with a
  *start* rather than an end. Nothing expires a plotted card; the turn it was
  plotted on is the one turn it may not be cast.
- **`playable_free`** — "without paying its mana cost". Priced as `FREE_COST`
  rather than as a discount, because 601.2b is not a reduction to zero and the
  difference shows on an X spell, where a discount leaves X payable.
- **`playable_sorcery_only`** — a restriction on the *permission*, not on the
  card. A plotted instant is still an instant and `_timing_ok` would happily
  offer it in response to something.

Both sides of the free cast read the same flag off the same card — legality
prices the line with it and `game._cast` pays with it — which is the argument the
`playable_any_type` block already makes one line down, and the bug the
`from_library_top` branch records: a line offered free and billed the printed cost
is a cast that silently does nothing.

### "If you do" needed nothing

The exile and the plotting are one rider, so there is no state in which the first
happened and the second did not. That is exactly what the printed conditional
says, and expressing it separately would have invented a failure mode the card
does not have.

### The one new piece: `min_colors`

"Multicolored" is two or more colors (202.2b). `colors` cannot say it — it is a
membership test, so `{"colors": ["U", "R"]}` matches a mono-red spell — and
`require_all` means exactly those colours and no others.

Written as a number rather than a `multicolored` boolean because the number is
what the rule says and reads the same on the rarer "three or more colors".
Honoured by all three matchers, since a filter that means one thing to a trigger
and another to a selector is worse than not having it: the selector language reads
the *derived* colours (so a repainted permanent is matched on what it is), and the
trigger filter and `_matches_printed` read the printed face, each for the reason
already written beside their `colors` clause.

`tests/unit/test_plot.py` keeps the mono-coloured instant as a live card, because
it is the card `colors` would have given.

## "Each of X targets" — an ordering rule, not a rewrite

### Overview

Crackle with Power: "{X}{R}{R}{R}. Crackle with Power deals 5 damage to each of X
targets."

I had flagged this as architecturally blocked twice, on the grounds that targets
are declared as part of casting while legality enumerates target tuples with X
pinned at 0. That was half right and the wrong half was the conclusion.

### The refusal was correct and its reason was not universal

`loader.targets._compile_targets` refuses a value-expression `count` on a card's
own `targets`:

> a spell's are declared while it is being cast (601.2c), before X is chosen and
> before any additional cost is paid, so the expression would read 0

That is exactly right for `{"additional_paid": true}` — kicker and replicate are
paid at 601.2h, long after targets. It is exactly wrong for X, because 601.2b
announces X and 601.2c declares targets, **in that order**.

### The flow already existed

`Game._cast` runs `_ask_x`, then `_ask_modes`, then `_ask_mode_targets`. That last
one declares a mode's own targets at cast time, after a cast-time choice, and its
docstring says why that is legitimate: "Runs immediately after `_ask_modes` and
before the spell is paid for, which is exactly where 601.2 puts it."

`_ask_x_targets` is that method's sibling with X in place of the mode list. No
casting-flow change, no new decision kind, no new event — the proposal I had been
carrying (one cast line per affordable X, bounded by a choice cap) would have
multiplied target tuples by a choice the player already makes a moment later, and
was strictly worse than the thing already in the file.

### Legality stays a gate

The comment beside the `x_count` check in `_cast_variant` had already settled this
for the cost:

> X is a *gate* here, not a value. Legality asks only "is there any X this is
> castable at", and `game._cast` then asks the player which one — so the action
> carries X = 0.

The target spec sizes to zero there for the same reason and the line is still
offered. Nothing about legality changed.

### `filter_legal` needed nothing at all

`TargetSpec.variable_size` already makes the last spec swallow whatever refs
remain, the loader already guarantees there is at most one and that it comes last,
and the comment already argues that re-evaluating a computed count on resolution
would be *worse* than using the stored length: "the number is fixed when the
targets are declared (601.2c), and anything that moved in between would re-slice
refs that were chosen under the old one."

That is the semantics an X-sized target wants, written before one existed.

### Two refusals kept

`{"x": true}` on a card with no `{X}` in its mana cost is a load error — the spec
would size to zero for ever, which is a spell that says it targets and never does,
the silent half of the mistake the original clause prevents. Every other computed
count on a spell is refused exactly as before.

## Sink into Stupor — two capabilities, one card

The last card in the Vivi deck, and it needed both faces built.

### "Target spell or nonland permanent an opponent controls"

One instance of the word "target" whose legal choices live in two zones at once.
`kind: "spell"` walks the stack; `"permanent"` and `"any"` walk the battlefield;
nothing pooled the two.

**One spec, not two.** Writing one of each kind is a card that targets *twice*:
it would need a legal choice of each to be castable at all, and 608.2b would
fizzle it if either became illegal. The printed card is castable with only a
permanent on the board and with only a spell on the stack.

`still_legal` needed no change whatever. It already re-checks a stored ref by
`ref.kind` rather than by the spec's kind, so every ref the new pool offers is one
it will accept — the design working rather than a lucky escape. The `selector`
narrows both halves, because "nonland" and "an opponent controls" are meant to.

What did need saying is where the chosen thing goes. `return_spell_to_hand` read
only `ctx.target_sids`, so a union target that landed on a permanent returned
nothing and left it on the battlefield with the card looking like it worked. That
is the exact silent failure that op's own docstring was written about — it argues
at length that `return_to_hand` "cannot see a spell" and is a silent no-op — one
kind further along, pointing the other way.

### "As this land enters, you may pay 3 life"

Steam Vents already ships in this pool with the sentence dropped. A land that
always enters tapped is a strictly worse card and nothing on the board says so,
which is the same silent-narrowing failure the impulse durations were about.

**Where the question is asked is the whole design.** 614 applies enters
replacements *inside* the zone change, and `move_object` is not a generator: it
cannot stop for a decision. The gap record proposed making that path suspend "the
way dredge/madness/miracle do", which would put a suspend point inside every zone
change in the engine — every death, every draw, every token.

The cheaper and more exact answer is to ask a moment earlier. Both paths that put
a permanent onto the battlefield are *already* generators — `game._play_land` for
a land drop, `stack._place_after_resolution` for a permanent spell — so
`zones.offer_enters_costs` is called there and leaves the answer on the object.

That is not an approximation. Nobody receives priority between the question and
the arrival, so there is no window in which the permanent exists with the question
unanswered. `_play_land` already makes exactly this argument for writing
`showing_second_face` before the move rather than during it.

`enters_cost_paid` survives `reset_permanent_state` deliberately — the same
exemption `hasted_by_suspend` has, and its comment gives the same reason, that the
flag is set a moment before a move this runs during. `_enter_battlefield` clears
it once the replacements have read it, because a permanent that leaves and comes
back is a new object (400.7) whose controller has been asked nothing.

**One divergence, stated:** an unaffordable price is never offered. 118.4 forbids
paying life you do not have, so a player at 2 life is not shown a question whose
"yes" cannot be honoured — which would otherwise leave the arrival depending on
how a failed payment was reported.

## `nth` on `spell_cast` — "their second spell", "their first noncreature spell"

### Overview

Five gap records named one capability: Esper Sentinel and The Queen of Dale
("whenever an opponent casts their first noncreature spell each turn"), Mangara,
the Diplomat and Trouble in Pairs ("…casts their second spell each turn"), and
The Council of Four ("a player casts their second spell during their turn").
Each is the question `nth` already answered for draws — *which* one was this, for
the player who did it — asked of a cast.

### Why the existing vocabulary would not do

- `max_per_turn: 1` is counted per permanent. "An opponent casts **their**
  first" is per opponent, so in a pod the first opponent's spell spends the cap
  and the second's first spell taxes nothing. It cannot say "second" at all.
- A `condition` on `spells_cast_this_turn` is re-asked on resolution (603.4). An
  opponent who casts their second spell and a third in response has moved the
  tally to 3 before the trigger resolves, and it is skipped. `>=` fires on every
  spell after. Both are the draw-ordinal argument again.
- A flat ordinal cannot say "noncreature": a creature then an instant is the
  first noncreature spell and the second spell.

### The shape

`GameState._tally` already bumped `spells_cast[pid]` on every SPELL_CAST; it now
writes the post-bump value onto the event as `data["nth"]`. The fold is the one
place all three cast paths pass through (`game._cast`, the alternative-cost cast
in `replacements.py`, suspend's free cast), so none can forget it.

`triggers._matches` compares `nth` through `_ordinal`. Unfiltered, that is the
event's value. With a `filter`, `_spell_ordinal` counts the caster's earlier
entries in `TurnLedger.spells_cast_ids` matching the filter — cut at this cast's
flat ordinal, so a later cast can never move an earlier one's place — and adds
one for this spell, which the trigger's own `filter` check has to accept anyway.

**Why the filter and not per-kind ordinals on the event:** the kinds are
open-ended — noncreature, instant or sorcery, multicolored — and a fixed set on
the event would be a vocabulary the next card outgrows. The printed family is
always "their Nth *kind* spell", so the kind the trigger already filters on *is*
the run it counts.

**Printed faces only.** The earlier spells have left the stack, so they are
matched with `_matches_printed`, the matcher the filtered
`spells_cast_this_turn` value already uses. A filter key that reads board state
would be applied to this spell and ignored on the earlier ones, so the loader
refuses anything outside `triggers.ORDINAL_FILTER_KEYS` on a `spell_cast`
trigger that carries `nth`.

### Tier A

No op, no `EventType` (the payload key rides on `spell_cast`), no decision kind,
no API field, nothing under `frontend/`. The loader guard widened from `draw` to
`draw` and `spell_cast`, and the authoring packet's note on `trigger_keys` now
says so, and says why `max_per_turn` is not "an opponent's first".

### Guarded by

`tests/unit/test_spell_cast_nth.py`: the ordinal on the event per caster; only
the second spell fires the unfiltered form, creature spells included; a third
spell in response does not hide it, while the `condition` encoding
(`t_nth_spell_condition`) resolves skipped; the noncreature run (a creature does
not fire it, an instant after a creature does, a second noncreature does not);
the run is cut at the cast; two opponents in a pod each fire it once; spells
cast before the watcher entered still count; "during their turn"; the turn
boundary; and the load-time guards.

The five cards are not authored in this change; their gap records stay until
they are re-authored. Esper Sentinel still needs nothing else; The Queen of Dale's
recruit is sayable with existing ops; Trouble in Pairs still needs extra turns.

## `extra_turn` and `skip_extra_turn` — "take an extra turn after this one"

### Overview

Three gap records named one missing concept: Perch Protection ("Gift an extra
turn"), Trouble in Pairs ("If an opponent would begin an extra turn, that player
skips that turn instead") and Final Fortune ("Take an extra turn after this
one"). The engine had no turn that was not the next live seat's —
`turn._begin_next_turn` advanced `active_idx` by one and that was the whole turn
order — so there was nothing for an op to add or a replacement to catch.

### Why the existing vocabulary would not do

- `extra_combat` and `extra_land_drop` add sub-steps *inside* the turn in
  progress, and `extra_phases` is cleared at the very boundary an extra turn has
  to cross.
- `skip_draw_step` is the closest static and suppresses a turn-based action
  inside a turn; it reaches nothing about the turn sequence.
- Writing Perch Protection's `gift` label and dropping the reward would pass
  every authoring gate and never hand over the promised turn.

### The shape

- **`GameState.extra_turns`**, a stack of player ids. Rule 500.7: added directly
  after the current turn, one at a time, APNAP order for several players, most
  recently created first. Popping from the end is all three, including a turn
  created during an extra turn landing ahead of the ones already waiting.
- **`GameState.turn_order_idx`**, the seat whose ordinary turn the table resumes
  after. Without it, a turn gifted across a pod would be followed by the seat
  after the *recipient*, skipping everyone between.
- **`extra_turn` op** (`ops_player.py`), usual player spec defaulting to `"you"`.
  `"gift_recipient"` already resolves to nobody on the unpromised line, so
  Perch Protection's reward is one unconditional entry, as Parting Gust's Fish
  is. The loader refuses `controller` on it by name — that is the key Parting
  Gust aims with, and copied here it would be ignored and give the caster the
  turn.
- **`skip_extra_turn` static**, player-wide with `affects_player`. A replacement
  (614.10) asked in `turn._take_extra_turn` as a queued turn would begin — not at
  scheduling, so a turn queued before the permanent arrived is still skipped and
  two queued turns are skipped one at a time. A skipped turn takes no turn number.
- An extra turn takes a turn number and counts against the turn cap, but does
  not complete a round.
- `GameState.previous_active` replaces day/night's "the seat to the right" as
  726.2's previous turn's active player, which an extra turn made wrong.

### Tier D

One new event, `turn_skipped`, since a skipped turn fires no `turn_began` and
would otherwise leave no trace. `turn_began` carries `extra: true` on an extra
turn only, so ordinary logs are byte-identical. Frontend: `describeEvent` reads
"-- Your extra turn 2 --" and "AI 1 skips an extra turn"; `beatsFor` banners
"Your Extra Turn" and a per-seat toned "skips their extra turn". No API field:
the scheduled stack is not serialized.

### Guarded by

`tests/unit/test_extra_turn.py`: Time Warp's sequence and the control; a turn but
not a round; `extra` only on extra turns; the recorded previous player; the gift
promised, unpromised, and across a pod; newest first, a turn created during an
extra turn, APNAP for "each player", an eliminated player's turn discarded; the
skip for an opponent but not its controller, never for ordinary turns, one at a
time, for a turn queued before it arrived, and not once it has gone; and the
loader guards. Frontend: `tests/labels.test.ts`, `tests/events.test.ts`.

No card is authored in this change and the gap records stay. Perch Protection
needs nothing else: `bird_2_2_u_flying` has since shipped, and its promised
branch is Teferi's Protection's three effects behind `gift_promised`; Trouble in Pairs' second line is
sayable now that `nth` on `spell_cast` has shipped; Final Fortune still needs a
delayed trigger scoped to the extra turn it created and a `lose_game` op.

## Copy exceptions — "except it's legendary", "…an artifact in addition", eternalize

### Overview

Rule 707.9b: a copy effect that modifies a characteristic "as part of the
copying process" makes that characteristic a copiable value of the copy.
`copy_permanent`'s `except_` already had embalm's `colors`, `add_subtypes` and
`no_mana_cost`, and Espers to Magicite's replacing `types`. It gains:

| key | printed clause | witness |
|---|---|---|
| `add_supertypes` | "except it's legendary" | Adagia, Windswept Bastion |
| `add_types` | "except it's an artifact in addition to its other types" | Faerie Artisans |
| `power`, `toughness` | eternalize's "except it's a 4/4 black Zombie …" | Champion of Wits |

### Why the existing vocabulary would not do

The loader refused every key outside the four, and `characteristics._compute`
applied only those. `types` replaces, so it cannot say "in addition"; nothing
in the DSL could touch a supertype; and `set_pt`/`animate` wear off at cleanup,
where a copiable value is permanent.

### The shape

All three are applied in `_compute` to the printed face before any layer, where
the rest of `copy_overrides` already was. The base size replaces the printed
P/T, so a counter on an eternalized token makes it a 5/5. The loader holds the
key set as `COPY_EXCEPT_KEYS` and refuses unknown supertypes and card types, an
empty addition, `types` with `add_types`, half a size, and a size that is not a
non-negative integer.

**The legend rule had to move.** `sba._legend_rule` read `card.is_legendary`
off the printed card, so a token copied "except it's legendary" would report
Legendary in `chars` and never be put into the graveyard. It now reads the
derived supertypes.

Eternalize needs no keyword: it is embalm's activated ability from the
graveyard with this bigger exception. Champion of Wits' printed line is Snake
Wizard, so `add_subtypes: ["Zombie"]` completes "Zombie Snake Wizard".

### Tier A

No op, no event, no decision kind, no API field, nothing under `frontend/`.
The authoring packet lists `except_` as a `copy_permanent` key, not its
sub-keys, so it needs no change.

### Guarded by

`tests/unit/test_copy_except.py`: the legendary token and the untouched
original, the legend rule keeping one of two legendary copies (and neither
without the clause), a legendary selector; the artifact copy that is still a
2/2 creature and is found by an artifact selector (and is not without the
clause); the eternalized token's 4/4 size, black colour, mana value 0, added
Zombie, a counter layering on top, and the original's size; and the load-time
guards.

The three cards are not authored in this change. Adagia, Windswept Bastion still
needs Station (a cost that binds the tapped creature's power, and the "12+ |"
threshold ability); Faerie Artisans still needs "tokens created with this
creature"; Champion of Wits needs nothing else.

## Draw tracking — "each opponent who drew a card this way"

### Overview

Cut a Deal: *"Each opponent draws a card, then you draw a card for each opponent
who drew a card this way."* One gap record, `draw-tracking`. `draw` recorded
nothing and the loader refused an `as` on it, so the second half had no honest
spelling.

### Why the existing vocabulary would not do

- `for_each_player` over `"each_opponent"` counts opponents at the table, not
  opponents who drew. It pays out for an opponent with an empty library (121.4:
  an attempt to draw is not a draw) and for one whose draw dredge replaced
  (121.6, 614.11). Both positions are reachable here.
- `cards_drawn_this_turn` is a turn-wide tally that also counts draw steps.
- `may`'s `as` is the only other seat-set binding, and wrapping a mandatory draw
  in a `may` hands each opponent a choice the card does not print.

### The shape

`op_draw` keeps what `replacements.draw` returns and, given an `as`, writes the
seats whose list was non-empty -- the list-of-player-ids shape `may` already
writes and the `{"binding": …}` player spec already reads (seat order, living
players only). It is written even when nobody drew, and accumulates across a
`for_each_player` loop as `may`'s does. `draw` joins `RECORDING_OPS`, which is
all the loader's `as` guard needed.

### The loader guard

`resolve_pool` reads any bound list as oids, so `{"count": {"binding": "drew"}}`
would load and count *objects* whose ids equal the seats. The new
`loader.effects._refuse_seats_read_as_objects` refuses a `draw` or `may` binding
under any object-pool key (`count`, `exists`, `objects`, `per`, `from`,
`attacker`, `source_object`) or in `exclude_binding`.

### Tier A

No new op, event, decision kind or API field; nothing under `frontend/`. The
authoring packet needed nothing: `as` is not a per-op vocabulary list there.

### Guarded by

`tests/unit/test_draw_tracking.py`: the seats recorded; an empty library not
recorded (and still flagged for the loss); a dredged draw not recorded and a
declined dredge recorded; fewer cards than asked still recorded; the empty
write; accumulation across a loop; the whole Cut a Deal effect list at two
players, with a decked opponent, and at a four-player pod with and without one;
and the load-time guards.

Cut a Deal is not authored in this change; its gap record stays until it is.

## `cant_cast_spells` — a player who may not cast, from anywhere, by any route

### Overview

Voice of Victory: *"Your opponents can't cast spells during your turn."* The
engine had two cast prohibitions and both were the wrong shape. Split second
(702.61a) is read off the stack, binds every player including its caster, and
ends when the spell leaves; epic (702.50a) is a card-level rider that locks its
own controller for the rest of the game. Neither can say "these seats, while
this permanent is here, during this turn". The near misses in the static
vocabulary were permissions and prices (`cast_from_graveyard`,
`spell_cost_reduction`, `attack_tax`) or a mana tax (`freeze_opponent_lands`),
and a `spell_cast` trigger that counters is not "can't cast": the spell is still
cast, still paid for, and still fires cast triggers.

### Where it is read

A player-wide static in `PLAYER_WIDE_STATIC_EFFECTS`, answered by
`player_statics.player_cant_cast_spells` through `_active_player_statics`, so
`affects_player` and the `condition` are honoured exactly as they are for
Bloodletter.

- **Legality.** `casting._cast_actions` returns nothing, beside epic's gate and
  before any zone is walked. 601.2 names no zone, so a gate in the hand loop
  would pass every hand test and let flashback straight through.
- **Resolution-time casts.** Rule 101.2: a "can't" beats a "may". Every cast a
  resolving effect makes goes through one of three places, and each refuses:
  `suspend.cast_for_free` (suspend, rebound, cascade, ripple, `cast_from_hand`,
  `play_exiled`, `look_at_top`'s `cast_free`), `replacements._offer_cast`
  (madness, miracle), and `op_cast_copy` — 707.12 makes casting a copy a cast,
  even though the engine builds it with `put_copy_on_stack`. `_offer_free_cast`
  and `cast_from_hand` check before asking, so no prompt is shown whose yes does
  nothing. The refused card stays where the no-legal-target outcome already
  leaves it: in exile for suspend and rebound, bottomed with the rest for
  cascade, exiled for madness.

### What it does not stop

Copies (`copy_spell`, storm, epic's upkeep copy — 707.10, never cast), playing a
land, the special actions suspend and foretell (116.2), and activated abilities.
Each is pinned, because a lock that also withheld one would be a strictly
stronger card that looks identical on the board.

### Refused at load

`affects_player` is required (as for every player-wide static), and `affects` or
`amount` beside `cant_cast_spells` is a load error: nothing reads them, so
"Your opponents can't cast creature spells" written with a filter would load as
a lock on every spell.

### Tier

A static and its readers: no op, no `EventType`, no decision kind, no API field,
nothing under `frontend/`. The AI needs nothing — its action mask is
`legality.legal_actions()`. The authoring packet's `static_effects` list is
derived from `STATIC_EFFECTS`, and a note now names the shape.

### Guarded by

`tests/unit/test_cant_cast_spells.py`: the opponent locked on your turn and free
on theirs; the turn passing and the source leaving both lift it; the controller
is unaffected; the unconditional twin locks either turn; flashback from the
graveyard is withheld; abilities, land drops and spell copies survive; an
opponent's cascade during your turn casts nothing and asks nothing, and the same
cascade on their turn casts; `cast_for_free` refuses directly; madness still
exiles but does not cast; cipher's cast-a-copy is refused, and allowed again on
their turn; and the load-time guards.

Voice of Victory is not authored in this change. Its Mobilize 2 line was already
expressible (`create_token` with `tapped`/`attacking`/`as` plus a `delay`ed
`sacrifice`), so the card is now fully answerable. Grand Abolisher, Drannith
Magistrate and Deafening Silence need a spell filter or an ability lock and
remain gaps.

## `no_maximum_hand_size` — "for the rest of the game", off a sorcery

### Overview

Sea Gate Restoration // Sea Gate, Reborn was blocked on its last sentence: "You
have no maximum hand size for the rest of the game." The catalogue prints the
same one-shot on Finale of Revelation and Ancient Silver Dragon.

### Why the existing vocabulary would not do

- `no_hand_limit` is a **static**, read through `_active_player_statics`, which
  walks the battlefield. A sorcery is never there, and a static in `abilities`
  on an instant or sorcery is never read.
- `grant_ability` cannot hand out a player-wide static, and there is no
  permanent to grant it to.
- `set_flag` writes onto an object, cleared on a zone change, and nothing in the
  cleanup step reads the flag ledger.

### The shape

- **`PlayerState.has_no_maximum_hand_size`**, one-way, beside
  `has_city_s_blessing` and `epic_source`, and on `PlayerState.to_dict`.
- **`no_maximum_hand_size`** in `effects/ops_player.py`: the ordinary player
  spec, defaulting to `"you"`, sets the flag on each seat named.
- **`player_statics.player_has_no_hand_limit`** returns True for the flag before
  asking the statics. `turn._cleanup_step` is unchanged: one reader, one rule
  path (514.1), and a Reliquary Tower leaving does not clear the one-shot.

### The loader guard

`duration`, `objects` and `controller` on the op are load errors. The lifetime
is the name; "until your next turn" (Enter the Infinite) would otherwise load
and play as permanent.

### Tier A

No event, decision kind or API field; nothing under `frontend/`. The packet's
`ops` and `op_options` are derived from the registry, so the op and its `player`
key reach workers without a hand-written entry. `tests/cards/golden_vocabulary.json`
gains the op name.

### Guarded by

`tests/unit/test_no_maximum_hand_size.py`: a nine-card hand survives cleanup,
with the no-spell control discarding to seven; the opponent still discards; an
`each_player` spec frees both; the spell is in the graveyard and the hand is
still kept on the caster's next turn; the flag is on the serialized view; a
Reliquary Tower alone still works and losing one does not clear the one-shot;
and the load-time guards.

Sea Gate Restoration is not authored in this change; its gap record stays until
it is.

## `replace_draw` — "if you would draw a card, draw two cards instead"

### Overview

Bard, King of Dale: *"If you would draw a card **except the first one you draw in
each of your draw steps**, draw two cards instead."* Thought Reflection prints the
plain form and Alhammarret's Archive prints Bard's exemption word for word, so one
static carries both:

```jsonc
{ "kind": "static", "effect": "replace_draw", "affects_player": "you",
  "draw_multiplier": 2, "except_first_in_draw_step": true }
```

The near miss is a `draw` **trigger** that draws one more. It fires after the
card is already in hand, can be responded to, fires again on its own draw, and is
a different card against anything that counts draws.

### Where it is applied

`replacements.draw` already took every draw after the opening hand one card at a
time, because dredge replaces *a* draw and miracle asks about the first card of
the turn. The doubler goes in the same per-card function, `_draw_one`: dredge is
offered, then the applicable doublers, then the actual draw and miracle. Per card
is required (121.2): the exemption is true of the draw step's first card and false
of its second, so "draw two" there is one card then two.

### The draw-step record

`state.cards_drawn_this_draw_step`, cleared at the top of `turn._draw_step` and
bumped in `primitives.draw_cards` only while `step is Step.DRAW`.
`cards_drawn_this_turn` cannot answer the question: a card drawn during upkeep
has already moved it, and the turn-based draw would then look like a second
draw and be doubled. Only the controller's own draw step exempts anything
("your draw steps"); their first draw during an opponent's draw step is doubled.
A draw replaced by dredge draws no card, so the next card is still the first.

### 614.5, 616.1

Each recursion carries the set of doubler sources that already replaced the draw
it came from. A doubler never re-doubles its own output, which also keeps the
recursion finite, and a second doubler applies to each of those draws, so two
Reflections make four. Thought Reflection beside Bard makes the turn-based draw
three: the first of Reflection's two draws is the step's first card and Bard
leaves it alone; the second is not.

Dredge against a doubler is the one ordering that can change the outcome, and it
is asked: dredge is offered on the original draw (taking it replaces the draw and
nothing doubles), and if declined it is offered again on each draw the doubler
made. Every order the player could choose is one of those paths. Two doublers
commute, so their order is not asked.

### Refused at load

`draw_multiplier` is required and at least 2. `affects_player` is required, as on
every player-wide static. `affects` and `amount` are refused, and so are
`draw_multiplier` and `except_first_in_draw_step` on any other effect.

### Tier

A static and its reader: no op, no `EventType`, no decision kind (dredge's
existing `ask_objects` question is re-used), no API field, nothing under
`frontend/`. The packet's `static_effects` and `ability_keys` are derived, and a
note names the shape.

### Guarded by

`tests/unit/test_draw_doubling.py`: the plain doubler on a draw, on draw two, on
the turn-based draw, and as two `DRAW` events; the bare primitive (the opening
hand) is not replaced. Bard's first draw-step draw is not doubled, the second is,
and "draw two" there is three; upkeep and main-phase draws are doubled; two cards
drawn in upkeep do not use up the exemption; each draw step's exemption is fresh;
a real turn through the turn walk draws one. The opponent is unaffected, and the
controller's draw during an opponent's draw step is doubled. Two doublers make
four; two Bards leave the draw step's first draw alone; Reflection with Bard
makes three. A doubled draw from a one-card library draws one and flags the
empty draw. Dredging the original draw skips the doubling, and declining then
dredging one of the two draws works. And the load-time guards.

No card is authored in this change. Bard, King of Dale still needs
`token_doubling` for its third line.

## Created-with-source — "tokens created with this creature"

### Overview

Faerie Artisans: *"Whenever a nontoken creature an opponent controls enters,
create a token that's a copy of that creature except it's an artifact in
addition to its other types. Then exile all other tokens created with this
creature."* One gap record, `created-with-source` (the copy's `add_types` half
landed separately).

### Why the existing vocabulary would not do

- `create_token` and `copy_permanent` recorded no creator: the token had an
  owner, a controller and `is_token`, and TOKEN_CREATED's `source` is the token
  itself.
- `as` does hold the copies, but a binding lives for one resolution and this
  clause reaches copies made by earlier triggers, turns ago.
- `{"is_token": true, "controller": "you"}` minus the fresh copy is a different
  card: it exiles every Treasure, Clue and Soldier you control, and a second
  Artisans' copy with them.

### The shape

Both ops pass `source=ctx.source_oid` to `primitives.create_token`, which adds
each token it makes (a replacement-substituted one included) to the source's
`GameObject.created_tokens` before the token enters. The `created_with: "self"`
selector key matches a candidate in the ability source's set, and
`triggers.matches_card_filter` honours the same key. "Other" is the op's `as`
binding through `exclude_binding`.

The record lives on the **creator**, not the token. The link is to this object
(the 607.2a linked-ability shape): a creator that leaves the battlefield and
returns is a new object (400.7), and the tokens its previous incarnation made are
no longer "created with this creature". An oid survives every zone change here,
so a pointer on the token could not tell the incarnations apart;
`reset_permanent_state` clears `created_tokens` on the move instead, at exactly
the moment the object ends. A token that left the battlefield has ceased to
exist (111.7) and is in no zone a selector searches, so the set is never pruned.

### The loader guard

`validate_selector` refuses any `created_with` value but `"self"`, which would
otherwise load and match no token.

### Tier A

No new op, event, decision kind or API field; nothing under `frontend/`. The
packet's `selector_keys` is derived from `SELECTOR_KEYS`, so workers are shown
the key with no packet change.

### Guarded by

`tests/unit/test_created_with_source.py`: the record written by `create_token`
and `copy_permanent`, the selector reading it and nothing written without a
source; Faerie Artisans end to end (`tests/data/created_with.cards.json`) — the
artifact copy, the earlier copy exiled on the next trigger, the just-made copy
surviving, another permanent's Treasure surviving (and exiled by the
`is_token` approximation, the counterfactual), and two Artisans each keeping
their own copy; a zone change clearing the record, a previous incarnation's copy
surviving while the new incarnation still exiles its own; the trigger filter;
and the load-time guard.

Faerie Artisans is not authored in this change; its gap record stays until it
is.

## `attacking_player` — "attacks you", not "attacks you and/or your planeswalkers"

### Overview

Trouble in Pairs: *"Whenever an opponent attacks you with two or more creatures,
draws their second card each turn, or casts their second spell each turn, you
draw a card."* One gap record, `attacking_player_selector`. Every other clause on
the card was already expressible; the attack clause was one creature too wide.

### Why the existing vocabulary would not do

- `creatures_attack_player` with `defending: "you"` binds `attackers` as every
  creature whose defending player is you. `combat.attackers[oid]` records the
  player even for an attack aimed at their planeswalker (`add_attacker` refuses
  a walker whose controller disagrees), so the binding is "you and/or
  planeswalkers you control" -- which is Mangara, the Diplomat, already shipped,
  and must keep meaning that.
- Rule 506.2 makes a player and each planeswalker they control separate attack
  targets (508.1b), so one creature at you and one at your planeswalker is one
  creature attacking you. Counting the bare binding draws a card the printed
  card does not.
- `attacking` is a bare boolean with no notion of whom, and nothing in the
  selector or value languages read `combat.attacking_planeswalker`.

### The shape

A selector key, `attacking_player: "you" | "opponent" | "any"`, relative to the
ability's controller. It matches a creature that is attacking (`combat.attacking`,
so a creature removed from combat does not), is **not** in
`combat.attacking_planeswalker`, and whose defending player the word names. Out
of combat it matches nothing. Trouble in Pairs' clause is:

```jsonc
"trigger": {
  "event": "creatures_attack_player", "controller": "opponent", "defending": "you",
  "condition": {"cmp": ">=",
    "left": {"count": {"binding": "attackers", "attacking_player": "you"}},
    "right": {"const": 2}}
}
```

A selector key rather than a trigger option because it composes: it narrows the
binding inside `count`, works on any battlefield pool, and needs no second
reading of the event. The predicate lives in one function,
`selectors.attacking_player_matches`, called from both `matches` and
`triggers.matches_card_filter` -- a trigger filter is validated against the same
`SELECTOR_KEYS`, and a key loaded there and ignored would be the silently-wider
filter.

### The loader guard

`validate_selector` refuses anything but the three words. `true` is the tempting
spelling (it is how `attacking` is written) and, read as a word, would name
nobody.

### Tier A

No new op, event, decision kind or API field; nothing under `frontend/`. The
authoring packet's `selector_keys` is derived from `SELECTOR_KEYS`, so workers see
the key with no packet change.

### Guarded by

`tests/unit/test_attacking_player_selector.py`: one at you and one at your
planeswalker counts 1 and does not fire; two at you counts 2 and fires; both at
the planeswalker counts 0; the Mangara reading of the same split still fires; at
a three-player pod, attacks at another opponent are not attacking you, and
`opponent`/`any` name the other seats without ever counting a planeswalker; the
trigger-filter half; nothing once combat ends; and the load-time refusals.

Trouble in Pairs is not authored in this change; its gap record stays until it
is.

## `crew_power_bonus` — crewing as though power were greater

### Overview

Shorikai, Genesis Engine: *"Create a 1/1 colorless Pilot creature token with
"This token crews Vehicles as though its power were 2 greater.""* Crew itself
shipped long ago (`tap_permanents` with `total_power`); what was missing was the
Pilot, and the Pilot was missing because its one printed line had no home. The
bodies nearest it (`gnome_1_1_c`, `hero_1_1_c`) are the wrong creature type and
drop the rider, and `buff` changes real power — a 3/1 that attacks for three.

### Where it is read

A static, `crew_power_bonus`, with `affects` and a required `amount`, answered
by `characteristics.crew_power_bonus` (summed over every applicable static, like
`prevented_damage`) and read by `costs._crew_power` — the renamed crew sum —
alone. That sum decides both whether the crew is offered (`_tap_cost_pool`) and
how much each creature takes off what is still needed as it is tapped (`pay`),
so a Pilot picked first against crew 3 ends the question. Nothing in the
characteristics pipeline sees it.

### The token

`pilot_1_1_c_crew2` in `data/cards/tokens.cards.json`: 1/1 colourless Pilot
creature, the static on `{"self_only": true}`. The authoring packet's
`token_ids` is derived from the pool, so it appears there with no further work.
The "saddles Mounts and crews" Pilot is a different token and is not defined:
the engine has no saddle.

### Tier

B-lite: a static and one reader. No op, no `EventType`, no decision kind, no API
field, nothing under `frontend/`. The AI's action mask is
`legality.legal_actions()`, which already reads the cost pool.

### Guarded by

`tests/unit/test_crew_power_bonus.py`: a Pilot and a 5/5 crew 8 and a vanilla
1/1 with the same 5/5 does not; a Pilot alone crews 3; the bonus belongs to the
Pilot and not to its companions; Hotshot Mechanic's nontoken copy of the line;
a tapped Pilot adds nothing; the bonus stacks with an anthem; paying taps both
creatures and stops as soon as the Pilot's crew power meets the number; the
Pilot is still a 1/1 and attacks for one; the created token is the printed
